members.name: dense
members.description: Tightens the trigger for dense layouts.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:
Where the open indicator sits, or whether there is one.

`auto` resolves to `end`, which is where a reader scanning a list of
summaries expects it: the label starts at the same x on every row, and the
indicator is found once at the edge rather than shifting with the text.
`start` is for a tree-like reading, where the indicator leads the label.
`none` is for a row that carries its own affordance and would otherwise
have two.

members.name: renderChevron
members.description: The chevron, or nothing when suppressed.

members.name: accordion
members.description:
The nearest accordion above this item, if there is one.

Resolved on demand rather than held, so an item moved between accordions
coordinates with the one it is in now. `closest` crosses no shadow
boundary, which is correct: an item inside another item's content is in
that item's light DOM and finds the same accordion, so the check below is
what keeps it independent.

members.name: peers
members.description:
The items this one coordinates with: its own siblings, and only those.

Direct children only. An accordion nested inside an item's content is a
separate set, and opening a section in it must not close anything outside.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Opens or closes this item, and enforces the accordion's mode.

The item that was clicked is the coordinator. It refuses first, then
announces, then applies, then closes its peers, in that order: closing a
peer before knowing whether this change was even allowed would leave the
set collapsed after a listener refused it.

members.name: focusTrigger
members.description:
Moves focus to this item's trigger.

The parent accordion drives arrow-key navigation and cannot reach the
trigger itself, because it is inside this item's shadow root. Exposing the
intent as a method keeps the parent out of the child's internals.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

the seam between two items is one pixel and not two. Those seams are what
carry the grouping, which is why the surrounding frame is opt-in rather than
the default: an accordion is a list, where a card is a surface.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
Whether the stack is framed.

- `plain` is the default and is what an application usually wants: the
  seams between items already say the items are one set, so a frame is a
  second statement of the same thing. Inside a card, a panel, a dialog or a
  sidebar, it is a line and no meaning.
- `outlined` frames the stack, for an accordion sitting directly on the
  page where nothing else says where it starts and stops. A marketing
  page's FAQ is the case it is for.

Both are writable, so a generated page can say which it means rather than
relying on the absence of an attribute.

members.name: mode
members.description:
How many sections may be open at once.

Absent is `multiple`, so nothing closes unexpectedly and the default costs
no attribute on the host. `single` keeps exactly one open and refuses to
close the last; `single-collapsible` keeps at most one and lets it close.

A union rather than a mode plus a `collapsible` boolean, which would make
`collapsible` alongside `multiple` expressible and meaningless.

members.description: Announces that it should go, and reports whether the request stood.

members.name: tone
members.description:
Which color the band wears.

**This was `severity` and it was claiming more than it did.** Severity is a
judgement about the message, and elsewhere in this library it carries one:
`Callout` reads `SEVERITIES` for an icon and a label, so `severity="danger"`
puts a mark beside the text and names it to a screen reader. Here it did
none of that. It set a color, the live region stayed polite either way, and
nothing about the announcement's semantics moved. A property that only
changes the paint should say so.

`tone` is the word this library already uses for exactly that, and `Tag`
made the identical rename for the identical reason: `appearance` is a
treatment, `tone` is semantic color. The set matches `Tag`'s so the two
agree, with `neutral` as the resting value and `primary` for a band that is
about the product rather than about a state.

`neutral` is what an unset announcement already looked like, said out loud
so a consumer can put a band back to it from markup, and `surface` is the
one value that is not a color: it lifts the band onto the surface step
instead of the sunken one, for a strip carrying something that is not a
state at all.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the `actions` region whether anything is in it.

An empty region is not free: it is still a flex item, so it still takes the
container's gap. There is no selector that can ask, `slot:empty` being
about a slot's fallback rather than its assigned nodes, so the component
asks and says so, on the region inside this shadow root rather than on the
host: an attribute written onto the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration and does not patch up.

declarations.description:
Flat, opaque, and in the flow. Both of the interesting things a banner can do
are opt-in: `sticky` because following the reader is a decision about the
page rather than about the bar, and `appearance="material"` because a
backdrop filter makes the header a containing block for `position: fixed`
descendants, so an overlay rendered inside a material header is placed
against the header rather than the viewport.

banner flat against a hero and lifts it off the content afterwards. There is
no shadow: the rule is the whole of it.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
How much of what is behind the banner shows through it.

One axis, three points, and `flat` is the default and the absent attribute.

- `flat` is opaque. The page stops at the bar, which is what an application
  wants: the bar is chrome and chrome does not need to be interesting.
- `material` is translucent and blurred, so content passing underneath
  stays visible and goes soft. The page reads as one surface with a bar
  floating over it.
- `transparent` has no fill at all until something has scrolled under it,
  and then it takes the flat one. For a banner over a hero, where the art
  should reach the top of the window and the bar should only become a
  surface once it has to be legible over moving content.

**`material` makes the header a containing block for `position: fixed`
descendants**, which is worth knowing and is narrower than it sounds. Every
overlay in this library goes into the top layer through the popover API or
`<dialog>`, and the top layer is not laid out against its DOM ancestors:
measured, a popover inside a blurred bar opens at the window origin while a
plain `position: fixed` child of the same bar opens at the bar's. So a
menu, a tooltip or a select in a material header is unaffected, and what is
caught is a consumer's own hand-positioned element.

members.name: sticky
members.description:
Whether the banner sticks to the top of the viewport.

Opt in, because following the reader is a decision about the page rather
than about the bar, and because a reflected `true` writes an attribute the
server's markup does not have. Every default here is the absent attribute.

It pairs with `appearance`: a bar that does not stick is only ever over the
top of the page, so `material` and `transparent` have nothing to be
translucent against and `data-scrolled` never lands.

members.name: navAlign
members.description:
Where the navigation sits in the bar.

Centered by default, which reads as the site's spine when the navigation is
the primary thing in the header rather than an afterthought beside a logo.
Centered against the banner rather than against whatever space the brand
left over, so the middle of the nav is the middle of the window whatever
the wordmark and the actions happen to measure.

`start` is the opt-out, for a header whose navigation trails the brand.

declarations.description:
They overlap by a step of space, which is enough to read as a stack without
the faces occluding each other. Each carries a ring in the page's own
background color, because a stack with no separation between its members
reads as one shape rather than several: the ring is what makes the edge of
each avatar visible against the one behind it.

Each avatar is drawn over the one before it, which falls out of document
order and needs no `z-index`. The familiar trick for putting the *first*
avatar on top is `row-reverse`, and it also reverses the row: the person
written first appears last. A facepile whose reading order is the reverse of
its markup is the worse trade of the two.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.description:
Says on the footer whether there is an attribution in it.

A `<footer>` with nothing in it is still a block in the quote's flow and
still takes the container's gap, so every blockquote written without an
attribution reserved a full space below itself. There is no selector that
can ask, `slot:empty` being about a slot's fallback rather than its
assigned nodes, so the component asks and says so on the footer inside this
shadow root: an attribute on the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration.

members.description:

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description:
The crumbs arrived, so measure them now that they are real.

The host renders and measures before its crumbs have upgraded, so every
width is zero and the arithmetic concludes that five crumbs fit in a
container half their size. Measured: `updated` ran once with
`widths: [0,0,0,0,0]`. `Tabs` carries the same paragraph for the same
reason, and its answer is this one, because a slot change is the moment
the children are real.

No `requestUpdate` here. `measure` asks for one when the answer moves,
which is the only time an update is owed.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
How much of its colour the button wears, which is how much it matters.

- `outlined` is the resting state and is never written: a line, a hairline
  wash inside it, and the label in the tone's own ink. Most buttons on most
  pages are this, and a page whose every button is filled has said nothing
  about which one matters.
- `solid` fills with the tone and puts the label on top of it, for the one
  action a region is for. There should be one.
- `subtle` is the tone as a wash with no line, for a button that should
  read as coloured without reading as the thing to press.
- `ghost` is the label alone until a pointer is over it: for actions that
  are available rather than suggested. Cancel, dismiss, a toolbar.

This is where emphasis comes from, rather than size: a filled button says
"this one matters" far louder than eight more pixels would.

**Independent of `tone`, which is the point of there being two.** Until
these were split, colour and fill were welded together as `primary`,
`secondary`, `tertiary` and `danger`: three of those are a rank and the
fourth is a meaning, so an outlined Delete and a Delete in a menu row could
not be written at all, and neither could a filled neutral. `Tag` reached
the same conclusion first and its note carries the longer argument.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What the button means, which decides its colour and nothing else.

- `neutral` is the resting state and is never written. The button is drawn
  in the page's own ink.
- `primary` is the brand colour, for the action a region is about.
- `danger` says the action is destructive before the confirmation does. The
  colour of the control is what a reader recognizes at a glance, where a red
  word inside a neutral button is something they have to read first.

Three and not six. `Tag` carries the full status set because a tag reports
a state, and a button performs an action: a success button and a warning
button are not things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page
where the colour of a control means nothing in particular.

members.name: variant
members.description:
One word for the four pairings anybody actually writes.

- `primary` is `appearance="solid" tone="primary"`.
- `secondary` is the resting button, and writing it says so out loud.
- `tertiary` is `appearance="ghost"`.
- `danger` is `appearance="solid" tone="danger"`.

**A spelling of the two axes, not a third thing beside them.** It exists
because the split cost a second attribute on the commonest control, and the
mapping lives in the stylesheet as extra selectors on the blocks that
already exist, so there is nowhere for the shorthand and the axes to drift
apart. Anything the four do not cover is written the long way, which is what
the axes are for: an outlined Delete is `appearance="outlined"
tone="danger"` and has no short name, because it is not one of four.

**An axis said out loud wins.** `variant="primary" appearance="ghost"` is a
ghost in the brand colour. That is the only reading of such markup that is
not a guess, and the selectors say it rather than relying on their order.

members.name: fill
members.description: How much of the space available to it the button takes. - `auto` is the default and is never written: the button is as wide as its label, which is what a control in a toolbar or beside a field should be. - `standard` is one width for every button that takes it, so a column or row of actions lines up instead of following the length of each word. - `full` fills the container, for a single action at the foot of a form or a card, and on a phone where a control is a target before it is a label. Width and not weight. `appearance` says how much a button matters and this says how much room it takes, and the three are independent: a `ghost standard` Cancel beside a `solid primary standard` Save is exactly the pairing a dialog wants. **A consumer's own anchor takes it as `data-button-fill`**, the way it takes the appearance as `data-button`: ```html Save ``` Both are one declaration in the base layer. They were not, and that was a real gap rather than a missing convenience: this class promises a link styled as a button and a real button are indistinguishable, and a dialog's button row is built on `standard`, so the one place the promise mattered most was the one place it did not hold.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a

carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

attributes.name: appearance
attributes.description:
How much of its colour the button wears, which is how much it matters.

- `outlined` is the resting state and is never written: a line, a hairline
  wash inside it, and the label in the tone's own ink. Most buttons on most
  pages are this, and a page whose every button is filled has said nothing
  about which one matters.
- `solid` fills with the tone and puts the label on top of it, for the one
  action a region is for. There should be one.
- `subtle` is the tone as a wash with no line, for a button that should
  read as coloured without reading as the thing to press.
- `ghost` is the label alone until a pointer is over it: for actions that
  are available rather than suggested. Cancel, dismiss, a toolbar.

This is where emphasis comes from, rather than size: a filled button says
"this one matters" far louder than eight more pixels would.

**Independent of `tone`, which is the point of there being two.** Until
these were split, colour and fill were welded together as `primary`,
`secondary`, `tertiary` and `danger`: three of those are a rank and the
fourth is a meaning, so an outlined Delete and a Delete in a menu row could
not be written at all, and neither could a filled neutral. `Tag` reached
the same conclusion first and its note carries the longer argument.

attributes.name: tone
attributes.description:
What the button means, which decides its colour and nothing else.

- `neutral` is the resting state and is never written. The button is drawn
  in the page's own ink.
- `primary` is the brand colour, for the action a region is about.
- `danger` says the action is destructive before the confirmation does. The
  colour of the control is what a reader recognizes at a glance, where a red
  word inside a neutral button is something they have to read first.

Three and not six. `Tag` carries the full status set because a tag reports
a state, and a button performs an action: a success button and a warning
button are not things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page
where the colour of a control means nothing in particular.

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:
One word for the four pairings anybody actually writes.

- `primary` is `appearance="solid" tone="primary"`.
- `secondary` is the resting button, and writing it says so out loud.
- `tertiary` is `appearance="ghost"`.
- `danger` is `appearance="solid" tone="danger"`.

**A spelling of the two axes, not a third thing beside them.** It exists
because the split cost a second attribute on the commonest control, and the
mapping lives in the stylesheet as extra selectors on the blocks that
already exist, so there is nowhere for the shorthand and the axes to drift
apart. Anything the four do not cover is written the long way, which is what
the axes are for: an outlined Delete is `appearance="outlined"
tone="danger"` and has no short name, because it is not one of four.

**An axis said out loud wins.** `variant="primary" appearance="ghost"` is a
ghost in the brand colour. That is the only reading of such markup that is
not a guess, and the selectors say it rather than relying on their order.

attributes.name: fill
attributes.description: How much of the space available to it the button takes. - `auto` is the default and is never written: the button is as wide as its label, which is what a control in a toolbar or beside a field should be. - `standard` is one width for every button that takes it, so a column or row of actions lines up instead of following the length of each word. - `full` fills the container, for a single action at the foot of a form or a card, and on a phone where a control is a target before it is a label. Width and not weight. `appearance` says how much a button matters and this says how much room it takes, and the three are independent: a `ghost standard` Cancel beside a `solid primary standard` Save is exactly the pairing a dialog wants. **A consumer's own anchor takes it as `data-button-fill`**, the way it takes the appearance as `data-button`: ```html Save ``` Both are one declaration in the base layer. They were not, and that was a real gap rather than a missing convenience: this class promises a link styled as a button and a real button are indistinguishable, and a dialog's button row is built on `standard`, so the one place the promise mattered most was the one place it did not hold.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description: What activating the button does to its form.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

attributes.name: command
attributes.description:

name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: indicatorPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the dots sit on.

Unset is `block-end`, under them. `block-start` puts them above,
`inline-start` and `inline-end` beside, where a run of dots becomes a
column.

**The sides of the content, not positions along a bar.** This was
`start | center | end`, which answered "where along the row" when the
question is "which edge", and could not say "above" at all. The logical
names rather than `top`/`left`, because the component is already careful
about writing direction everywhere else and an `inline-start` carousel
should put its dots on the right in Arabic without being told.

Independent of `controlsPlacement`. Both default to the block end, where
they share the row and split it, dots to the start and arrows to the end.
That is the arrangement the old shared bar gave, arrived at by two defaults
rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

members.name: indicatorAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

members.name: controlsPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

members.name: controlsAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

members.name: perView
members.description:
How many slides are shown across the track at once. Absent shows one.

No default, because it reflects. A reflected property with a value writes
its attribute on upgrade, and the host then carries something a consumer's
server markup never had, which React reports as a mismatch. The one-across
case is the absent attribute, and the styles read it that way.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the carousel.

members.name: index
members.description:
The slide in view, counted from zero.

Reading gives the real slide, in either mode. Writing sets it, the way a
script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an
`index` by then: declared, and the consumer owns it and the carousel only
announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

The same contract the four mixins carry, written out here rather than
extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the track runs.

Behavior rather than presentation, which is why it is here: the scroll
position and the nearest-slide arithmetic are both single-axis, and a
styled-tier attribute cannot change which one they read. Two sites branch
on it, `scrollTo` and the drag settle, and nothing else in the component
knows about the axis at all.

A vertical track needs a height, which a horizontal one does not: width
comes from the page and height does not, so the styled tier gives it
`--carousel-block-size` and a consumer sets that to whatever the slides
want.

members.name: defaultIndex
members.description: Slide to start on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: indexState
members.description: The slide in view, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: indexMode
members.description: Whether the consumer owns the slide, decided once and then fixed.

members.name: loop
members.description: Whether moving past either end wraps to the other.

members.name: autoplay
members.description: Whether the carousel advances on its own.

members.name: interval
members.description: How long each slide is held, in milliseconds.

members.name: rotating
members.description: Whether rotation is running. Absent until autoplay starts it.

members.name: slides
members.description: The slides, in light-DOM order. Empty on the server, which has no tree.

members.name: handleIndicatorKeydown
members.description:
The arrows move between indicators, which is the tablist pattern.

One tab stop for the set and the arrows within it, so a reader does not
have to press Tab once per slide to get past a carousel of twelve. Moving
changes the slide, because an indicator that could be focused without
selecting would leave the highlight and the slide disagreeing with nothing
on screen saying which is which.

members.name: goTo
members.description: Moves to a slide, wrapping only where `loop` says to.

members.name: settling
members.description:
Whether the scroll now settling is one this component asked for.

Cleared by the first `scrollend` after it is set, and by a reader taking
hold of the track. The second half is not belt and braces: a `scrollTo`
whose target is already the scroll position fires no `scrollend` at all,
and the clamped end of a `per-view` track is exactly that case. Measured:
clicking past the last reachable slide moves `index` and produces no
`scrollend`, so a flag that only a `scrollend` could clear would stay set
and swallow the reader's next drag.

members.name: stop
members.description:
Stops rotation for good.

Hovering away or moving focus out does not start it again. The APG is
explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks for it, because a
carousel that starts moving again on its own is the thing the control
exists to escape.

members.name: runTimer
members.description:
Owns the timer, from the state rather than from the call site.

`start()` and `stop()` each held the interval and `connectedCallback`
started one, which the rules forbid: a DOM move re-ran connect and restarted
rotation the reader had stopped, and the server, which never runs connect at
all, rendered the control saying the opposite of what it would do. The
state is what is declared and the timer follows it, which also means one
place clears it.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
Reads where a reader's drag settled, and only a reader's.

**The scroll we issued ourselves ends with a `scrollend` too, and taking it
as a reading is what makes the dots jump back.** This ran on every one, so
the index a reader had just chosen was overwritten by whichever slide
happened to be nearest the leading edge at the moment the animation
finished. Any disagreement there is enough: a snap settling a pixel short of
a midpoint, a target clamped by the scroller's own maximum, a fractional
layout, or a smooth scroll cut off by the next click. The component asked
for slide four, the pixels said three, and the pixels won.

Which is the wrong precedence in one direction only. A drag is the reader
moving the track and the index has to follow it; a click is the reader
moving the index and the track has to follow *that*. One `scrollend` cannot
tell those apart, so the flag does.

members.name: stopped
members.description:
Whether the reader has stopped it, as opposed to something pausing it.

The two were one flag and the difference matters: `focusin` bubbles, so
every focus move inside the carousel re-ran `stop()`, and a reader who
pressed Start had it undone by their very next Tab. Pausing on hover and on
focus is right; forgetting that the reader asked it to stop is not, and the
APG is explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks.

members.name: pause
members.description: Pauses without forgetting that the reader wanted it running.

rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

attributes.name: indicator-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

attributes.name: controls-placement
attributes.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

attributes.name: controls-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

attributes.name: per-view
attributes.description:
How many slides are shown across the track at once. Absent shows one.

No default, because it reflects. A reflected property with a value writes
its attribute on upgrade, and the host then carries something a consumer's
server markup never had, which React reports as a mismatch. The one-across
case is the absent attribute, and the styles read it that way.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the carousel.

attributes.name: index
attributes.description:
The slide in view, counted from zero.

Reading gives the real slide, in either mode. Writing sets it, the way a
script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an
`index` by then: declared, and the consumer owns it and the carousel only
announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

attributes.name: orientation
attributes.description:
Which way the track runs.

position and the nearest-slide arithmetic are both single-axis, and a
styled-tier attribute cannot change which one they read. Two sites branch
on it, `scrollTo` and the drag settle, and nothing else in the component
knows about the axis at all.

A vertical track needs a height, which a horizontal one does not: width
comes from the page and height does not, so the styled tier gives it
`--carousel-block-size` and a consumer sets that to whatever the slides
want.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: value
members.description: The checked values, comma separated.

members.name: boxes
members.description: The boxes, in light-DOM order. Client only: the server has no tree.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Pushes the group's name and value onto the boxes.

As properties rather than attributes. A `name` written onto a box is a
change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up. A box that names itself keeps its own.

members.name: seed
members.description:
Reads the boxes' own state into `value`, once, before anything is pushed.

`sync` used to refuse to write anything while `value` was empty, and the
guard was there for this: a group written with no `value` and boxes that
declare their own `checked` would have had them all cleared on the first
update. What it also did was make `group.value = ''` do nothing at all, so
the obvious way to clear a group silently did not, and the last box could
not be unticked through the group either.

Seeding is the honest version of the same intent. The markup decides the
starting set, exactly as before, and from then on `value` is what the boxes
follow, including when it is empty. The group's `value` is a derived read
of the boxes rather than state it owns, so reading it out of them at the
start is what it already means.

members.name: handleToggle
members.description:
Reads a box's requested change into `value`, and says so once.

The box is found from the event's target, which does two things. It tells
the group which box asked, where the detail carries only the shared name.
And it ignores the group's own dispatch, which lands on this same listener
because the group is what it is dispatched from: without the guard the
group answers itself until the stack gives out.

The requested state comes from the event rather than from the box. Driving
the boxes from `value` makes them controlled, so a controlled box applies
nothing on its own and reports what it was asked for. Reading `checked`
here would read the state it still holds and nothing would ever change.

members.name: validate
members.description:
Refuses an empty set where one was required, which nothing did.

`required` arrives with `MixinField`, reflects, and paints the asterisk
through the composed field sheet, and enforced nothing at all: no validity,
no message, and nothing cascading to the boxes. A group marked required
submitted empty.

**The group is form-associated, and submits nothing.** It was not, on the
reasoning that its boxes are the controls and each submits itself, which is
still true: nothing here calls `setFormValue`, so the set that reaches the
server is exactly the boxes it always was. What form association buys is the
other half of participation, validity, and there is no other mechanism for
it: `setValidity` throws `NotSupportedError` on an element the platform does
not know is a control.

So the fix that was written for "a group marked required submitted empty"
threw on every update in a real browser, and happy-dom's shim does not
throw, so the specs passed and the behaviour never worked. Eleven of them
failed the moment they were run in Chromium. It is also what makes the rest
work: the form now refuses to submit, which fires `invalid`, which is what
marks the field touched and puts the message on screen.

Anchored on the list, because the browser needs somewhere to point the
bubble.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: appearance
members.description:
How the choice presents itself.

- `plain` is the default and is never written: a box beside its words,
  which is what a list of choices should be almost always.
- `card` puts it in a bounded surface, for options that need room to
  explain themselves: a description, an icon, a price. It is the half a
  `data-card` link cannot do, because a link reports no value and belongs
  to no group, so a card that is genuinely an answer has to be this.

The box stays in both. A card whose only marker was its own border would
ask a reader to compare surfaces across a row to find the answer, and would
leave nothing for a high-contrast display.

members.name: checked
members.description:
Whether the control is checked.

One property rather than two. Reading gives the real state whichever
mode the control is in; writing hands ownership to the consumer, which
is what the attribute in `<helix-checkbox checked>` does as well. The
same shape all four of these mixins have, for the reason given on
`MixinControllerOpen.open`.

Not reflected: the attribute is the consumer's input and stays as they
wrote it, and `data-checked` carries the resolved state for stylesheets.

members.name: defaultChecked
members.description: Initial checked state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: checkedState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: checkedMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `checked` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestChecked
members.description:
Requests a checked change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-change` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode
the element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing
and waits for the consumer to pass a new `checked`, which is what
"controlled" means.

members.name: toggleChecked
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the control when the browser brings a form back.

Hand-written on the checkbox and nowhere else, so `Switch`, the mixin's
only other consumer, had no restore at all: a reader who navigated away
and came back to a restored form found their switch flipped off. The
mixin owns `checked`, so the mixin owns putting it back.

Through `checked` rather than the private state, so a controlled consumer
is asked the same way every other change asks.

members.name: resetChecked
members.description:
Drops the uncontrolled state, so the control reads `defaultChecked`
again.

A form reset has to return a control to what its markup declared, and
clearing `checked` alone only leaves controlled mode. The value the
element has been keeping lives here, so this is where it is dropped.

its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: indeterminate
members.description:
Whether the box shows as neither checked nor unchecked.

Presentation only. It never submits, and the first change resolves it.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated to the input, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value and the validity the host stands behind.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description: Returns the box to the state its markup declared.

members.name: handleLabelChange
members.description:
Whether there is a label to leave room for, written to the host.

The row is a flex line with a gap in it, so a label span rendered empty is
still a box and still takes that gap: an unlabelled box came out with eight
pixels of nothing after it. The input answers this by not rendering the
element, which cannot work here, because a checkbox is named by its own
content and the property is only that slot's fallback. Gating on the
property would unlabel every `<helix-checkbox>Text</helix-checkbox>` ever
written.

So the slot is asked instead, the same way `Tooltip` asks its own: with
`flatten`, because here the fallback counts, being where the property
renders. Client only, so a server-rendered unlabelled checkbox carries the
gap for one frame. That is a control with no accessible name, which has a
worse problem than its spacing.

members.name: syncLabelPresence
members.description:
Asks the slot, and says the answer on the host.

Called on `slotchange` and after every update, and the second is not
belt-and-braces: **`slotchange` does not fire when nothing is assigned.**
So a checkbox labelled only by its property, which is most of them, never
heard about its own label and rendered without one. Caught by the spec that
asks a labelled row to be wider than a bare one.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.
