attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
What it is called, and says, before a press.

Defaulted rather than left empty. An icon-only control must be named, and
the name of this one is not a judgement call: every copy button in the
world is called Copy. A consumer with a better word still sets it.

attributes.name: copied-label
attributes.description:
What it is called, and says, after one.

`attribute` written out, because Lit lowercases a property name rather than
dash-casing it, and `copiedlabel` is not what anyone would type.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description: What activating the button does to its form.

attributes.name: command
attributes.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

attributes.name: commandfor
attributes.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to

tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where

declarations.description:
The frame is the field rather than the input, so the trigger sits inside the
same box as the text and the focus ring is drawn once around the whole
control. The trigger is a mark within that box rather than a button beside it:
a second frame inside the first is two controls where a reader sees one.

The calendar is the real `helix-date-picker`, in a panel with no border of its
own. A surface over the page is told apart by its shadow and by what it
covers, and a line around it as well reads as a box drawn around something
already separate.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: mode
members.description:
How many dates can be held at once.

Absent is one. `range` holds a start and an end, `multiple` holds any
number, and both are carried as one comma-separated value: a form field
submits a string, and two fields for one question is a different control.

members.name: months
members.description:
How many months the calendar shows, side by side.

Worth more than one mainly for a range, where picking a start in March and
an end in April otherwise means paging between them and losing sight of the
first. The panel is sized by its content, so this widens it.

members.name: maxTags
members.description:
How many dates are shown as tags before the rest are counted, in `multiple`.

`0` is all of them, and is the default: a cap that guesses is worse than no
cap, because the number that fits depends on the width of the field and the
length of what is in it, neither of which this element knows. What a cap is
genuinely for is a field in a row or a table cell, where a set of twelve
dates would push everything below it down a line at a time.

The remainder is counted rather than hidden. "3 more" is a fact a reader can
act on, where a row that silently stops is a field that appears to have lost
what was put in it, and the count is what tells them there is more to see.

members.name: min
members.description: Earliest date that can be chosen, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

members.name: max
members.description: Latest date that can be chosen, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

members.name: disableDates
members.description: Dates that cannot be chosen, as a comma-separated `YYYY-MM-DD` list.

members.name: disableDays
members.description: Days of the week that cannot be chosen, `0` for Sunday through `6`.

members.name: firstDayOfWeek
members.description: First column of the week in the calendar, `0` for Sunday through `6`.

members.name: dateStyle
members.description:
How a date is written in the field: `short` through `full`, or ISO.

**The field renders when it is idle and holds the value when it is being
edited.** A written date is a rendering, and a document being edited must
not be a rendering of something else: `Intl.DateTimeFormat` formats and does
not parse, so `4 August 2026` cannot be typed back, and writing a parser per
locale is how a field ends up rejecting what it just displayed.

The way out is not to choose between the two but to separate them in time.
Idle, the field shows `4 August 2026`, which is what a date is for reading.
Focused, it shows `2026-08-04`, which is what a date is for typing, and it
goes back on the way out. Nothing parses a rendering, and nothing is
read-only, which is what an earlier version of this settled for.

A range is the exception that needs no swap: the dash between its two dates
is a separator this element understands, so that much reads back either way.

`iso` turns the rendering off, for a field whose reader is entering data
rather than reading it, or where the ISO form is itself the point.

The value is always `YYYY-MM-DD` regardless, because that is what a form
submits and what `min` and `max` compare against.

members.name: locale
members.description: Language tag the calendar names its months and days in.

members.name: placeholder
members.description: What the field says before a date is in it.

members.name: triggerLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the control that opens the calendar.

members.name: panel
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="field"]'), /* The surface *and* the trigger. * * A control is not always one element: the button that opens this panel is * part of it, and a press on it is not a press outside. Scoped to the * surface alone, `pointerdown` on the trigger closed the panel and the * trigger's own `toggleOpen` reopened it on the `click` that followed, so * the panel could never be closed by the button that opened it. Measured * across all five popover-bearing components: Menu, Popover and Tooltip * already named their invoker; this one and its three siblings did not, and * all four stayed open on a second press where Menu closed. * * `DismissController` documents this exact failure and takes a list for it. * The list was the fix; using it was the part that did not happen here. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null | undefined)[] => [ this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="trigger"]'), ], /* Wider than the four every other panel here takes. Those sit against a control the same width as themselves and read as an extension of it; this one is a calendar of its own size hanging off a field, so the gap is what says the two are separate things rather than one control that grew. */ offset: () => 8, onDismiss: () => this.requestOpen(false), placement: 'bottom-start', surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="surface"]'), })
members.description:
The overlay, placed against the field rather than the trigger.

Against the field because that is the box a reader sees as the control: a
calendar hung off a small button at one end of a wide field reads as
belonging to the button. `Select` anchors to its trigger for the opposite
reason, its trigger being the whole control.

members.name: picked
members.description:
What the calendar should show, which is only ever a whole date.

Half-typed input reaches here on every keystroke, and `2026-08-1` is not a
date: handing it to the calendar would move the month under a reader
mid-word. So the grid follows the field only once the field says something
complete.

members.name: written
members.description: One date, written the way `dateStyle` asks for.

members.name: editing
members.description: Whether the caret is in the field, which is when it holds the value.

members.name: draft
members.description:
What is being typed but not yet held, for `multiple` only.

The other modes type into the value directly, because one date and a range
are both a whole answer at the moment they are complete. A multiple is not:
it is a set being added to, so the field needs somewhere to hold a date
before it joins the set and somewhere to leave a half-typed one that is not
a date yet.

members.name: handleInput
members.description: Relayed under this element's name, so a consumer hears one control.

members.name: handleDraftKey
members.description: Adds what was typed to the set, or takes the last one back out.

members.name: shownDates
members.description: The dates that get a tag, which is all of them until `maxTags` says not.

members.name: restCount
members.description: How many are held beyond the ones shown.

members.name: removeDate
members.description: Takes one date back out of the set.

members.name: restore
members.description:
Puts the field back where the answer differs from what was typed.

`requestValue` is the mixin's, and it announces and decides; this is the
other half, which `Input` needs for the same reason: the native control has
already changed, so wherever the answer does not follow it, it has to be
restored. A refusal and a consumer who owns `value` and has not given a new
one are the same thing from here.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the value and the validity the host stands behind.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description: Escape shuts the calendar without moving the date.

members.name: returning
members.description:
Puts the caret back in the field without the field reopening the calendar.

Focus opens the calendar, so handing focus back after a pick reopens the
thing that was just answered. `relatedTarget` was the guard and it is not
enough on its own: it catches a hand-off from the trigger, and it does not
catch this, because the cell that had focus is gone by the time the caret
moves and the document has fallen back to something outside this element.

**Reasoned rather than measured, and worth saying which.** In a focused
document: the reader presses a day, the cell has focus, the panel is hidden,
the browser moves focus off the removed cell to the body, and the caret is
then put back here with `relatedTarget` pointing at the body, which is
outside this element and reads as an arrival. Every step is ordinary browser
behavior and none of it can be exercised here: `focus()` dispatches no
event in an unfocused document, which is what both the test runtime and the
available browser pane are. A spec was written for it and passed with the
guard removed, so it was covering nothing and has been taken out rather than
left to look like proof.

A flag rather than a better guess, because this element is the one moving
the focus and is the only thing that can know so. Cleared synchronously,
since `focus()` dispatches before it returns.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the caret in the field, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to

described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry

What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

attributes.name: months
attributes.description:
How many months the calendar shows, side by side.

an end in April otherwise means paging between them and losing sight of the
first. The panel is sized by its content, so this widens it.

attributes.name: max-tags
attributes.description:

`0` is all of them, and is the default: a cap that guesses is worse than no

length of what is in it, neither of which this element knows. What a cap is
genuinely for is a field in a row or a table cell, where a set of twelve

act on, where a row that silently stops is a field that appears to have lost

attributes.name: date-style
attributes.description:
How a date is written in the field: `short` through `full`, or ISO.

**The field renders when it is idle and holds the value when it is being
edited.** A written date is a rendering, and a document being edited must
not be a rendering of something else: `Intl.DateTimeFormat` formats and does
not parse, so `4 August 2026` cannot be typed back, and writing a parser per
locale is how a field ends up rejecting what it just displayed.

The way out is not to choose between the two but to separate them in time.
Idle, the field shows `4 August 2026`, which is what a date is for reading.
Focused, it shows `2026-08-04`, which is what a date is for typing, and it
goes back on the way out. Nothing parses a rendering, and nothing is
read-only, which is what an earlier version of this settled for.

A range is the exception that needs no swap: the dash between its two dates
is a separator this element understands, so that much reads back either way.

`iso` turns the rendering off, for a field whose reader is entering data
rather than reading it, or where the ISO form is itself the point.

The value is always `YYYY-MM-DD` regardless, because that is what a form
submits and what `min` and `max` compare against.

declarations.description:
Six week rows always, so the grid keeps one height and a month change does
not move whatever sits beneath it.

The column track is wider than the day, and the day is centered in it. The
difference is the space between days, which belongs to the track rather than

quieter rather than hidden, so the first and last weeks are whole and the
grid reads as a continuous run of dates.

members.name: valueMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `value` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description: Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says otherwise.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the control then
updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and waits for the
consumer to pass a new `value`, which is what controlled means.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.description: The selected dates, in order.

members.description: The month being shown, resolved from `month`, then `value`, then today.

members.name: derivedMonth
members.description:
The month to open on when nothing has declared one.

Split out from `shown` so `month` can report what is on display without the
two calling each other: `month` reading `shown` and `shown` reading `month`
is a stack overflow, and the specs found it immediately.

members.name: anchor
members.description:
The date the tab stop sits on, which is where the arrows move from.

It has to be a date the grid actually renders, so the month is compared
with its year. Comparing the month alone puts the stop on the same date a
year away, which is rendered nowhere, and the grid is left with no tab stop
at all and no way into it from the keyboard.

Each candidate is tested in turn rather than the first one winning
outright. Where the last date focused is in some other month, the selected
date still holds the stop, and only with neither in view does it fall to
the first of the month.

members.name: weeksOf
members.description: Six weeks of dates, so a grid does not change height between months.

members.name: barred
members.description:
Whether a date is barred, by bound, by weekday, or by name.

`barred`, not `disabled`: the calendar is a form control now, and
`HelixFormElement.disabled` is a boolean about the whole control. A method
and a flag cannot share a name, and of the two it is the method that should
move, because "disabled" on a control means one thing everywhere else in
the library.

members.name: show
members.description:
Moves the view, announcing it first.

`helix-navigate` and not `helix-change`: paging chooses nothing, and a
consumer driving the view has to hear that it moved without being told the
answer did. In controlled mode nothing moves and the consumer decides,
which is the point of them holding it.

members.name: select
members.description:
Adds a date to the selection, as the mode allows.

`range` starts over once it holds two, so a third click begins a new range
rather than extending or replacing an end at random. `multiple` toggles, so
clicking a chosen date takes it out.

members.name: report
members.description:
Reports the dates to the form, one entry each.

`FormData` rather than the comma-joined string the property holds, because
`mode="multiple"` is genuinely several answers and a server reading
`dates=2026-08-04,2026-08-06` has to know to split it on a convention this
library invented. One entry per date is what every other multi-valued
control on the platform sends, and `range` sends its two the same way, in
order, so start and end arrive as the pair they already are.

**Nothing at all without a `name`, and that is the mechanism rather than a
detail.** It is what lets a calendar sit inside something that owns the
form value, which is how `DatePicker` will hold one. The guard has to be
explicit here in a way it does not for `Listbox`: a control reporting a
plain string is skipped by the form when it has no name, but a `FormData`
carries its own names and its entries are appended whatever the element is
called, so an unnamed calendar would submit empty-named dates.

members.name: monthCount
members.description:
How many months are shown, clamped once.

`months` was clamped at the call site and read raw where the last month is
identified, so a zero, a negative or a non-numeric value rendered nothing
and took the forward control with it: `index === this.months - 1` is never
true for `NaN`. One getter both read.

members.name: cachedFormats

type.text:
| {
        full: Intl.DateTimeFormat
        heading: Intl.DateTimeFormat
        locale: string
        weekday: Intl.DateTimeFormat
      }
    | undefined

members.description:
The three date formatters, built once per locale rather than per render.

`Intl.DateTimeFormat` is expensive to construct and these depend on nothing
but `locale`, and they were built inside the per-month render: three
constructions for every month on show, on every update, so a two-month
calendar rebuilt six of them each time an arrow key moved the anchor.
Measured elsewhere at about a quarter of a millisecond apiece, which is not
a crisis and is pure waste.

Keyed on the locale so a change to it is picked up, which a plain lazy
field would not do.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the dialog.

members.name: persistent
members.description:
Whether Escape can close it.

Off for a dialog that must be answered. It does not disable the close
control a consumer slots in: refusing to be dismissed is not the same as
refusing to be closed, and a dialog with no way out at all is a trap.

Escape *and* a press on the backdrop, which it now genuinely means. The
sentence said both for a long time while nothing listened for a backdrop
press, so it promised a behavior a consumer would have written their
markup around; the fix then was to narrow the sentence, and the fix now is
to build the half that was missing.

A persistent dialog does not ignore that press. It answers it: see
`refuse`, which is the only way a dialog that will not be dismissed can say
so at the moment a reader asks.

members.name: commands
members.default: new CommandController(this, { commands: { '--close': () => this.close(), '--show': () => this.show(), '--toggle': () => this.toggleOpen(), }, })

members.name: dialog
members.description: The native dialog, or nothing where there is no DOM to hold one.

members.name: show
members.description: Moves focus into the dialog and makes the rest of the page inert.

members.name: close
members.description: Asks to close, which a consumer may refuse.

members.name: handleCancel
members.description:
Escape, intercepted so it is a request rather than an act.

The native `cancel` event fires before the dialog closes, so preventing it
leaves the dialog open and lets `requestOpen` decide. Without this a reader
pressing Escape would close a dialog its consumer had said was open, and
the two would disagree until something else moved.

members.name: handleClose
members.description:
A close that happened anyway, reflected back.

`<form method="dialog">` closes the dialog directly and there is no event
to prevent. Rather than fight it, the state follows: the dialog is shut, so
saying otherwise would be a lie the next `showModal()` would trip over.

members.name: handleBackdrop
members.description:
A press on the backdrop, which lands on the dialog element itself.

**The target alone is not enough here, where it is for `Drawer`.** A modal
`<dialog>` attributes backdrop clicks to itself, which is the usual trick,
and this panel also carries `--dialog-inset` of padding: a press in that
padding has the same target as a press on the backdrop, so the trick alone
closes a dialog when a reader clicks just inside its own edge. The drawer
escapes that because its panel is flush against the window and its content
fills it. So the point is compared against the panel's box.

members.name: refuse
members.description:
Says no to a dismissal, by moving.

A persistent dialog that ignores a press on the backdrop is
indistinguishable from one that did not notice, and a reader's next move is
to press again harder. A short swell and settle is the smallest thing that
reads as "I heard you, and no": it is the same gesture a native alert makes
on macOS and the one every reader has already been taught.

An attribute for the length of the animation rather than a class, cleared
on `animationend`, so the styled tier decides what refusing looks like and
this decides only when it happens. Removed first so a second press
restarts it: without that, pressing twice does nothing the second time,
which is the impression the whole thing exists to avoid.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: orientation
members.description: Which way the rule runs.

members.name: announced
members.description:
Whether the rule is announced as a separator.

Off by default, and out of the accessibility tree. Most rules on a page
separate nothing: they underline a heading or close a section that space
had already closed, and announcing every one as a separator is noise a
screen-reader user has to walk past.

An opt-in, not a `decorative` opt-out, because a boolean attribute cannot
be turned off: `decorative="false"` parses as `true`, which would put the
quiet default out of reach from HTML and leave it settable only as a
property. An opt-in is absent by default, which every reflected property
here has to be.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Marks the middle region when nothing has been set into it.

A divider with no content has to be one continuous line, and the space
either side of the content is what would break it. `:empty` cannot answer
this and neither can `:host(:has(...))`, which is invalid CSS dropped at
parse time: `check:selectors` caught exactly that rule here, written in
this file, by an author who had already read the note saying so.

On the region inside the shadow root rather than on the host, because an
attribute written onto the host is a change to markup the consumer rendered.

members.description:
Which edge the drawer comes from.

Unset is `end`, which the styled tier reads as `:host(:not([placement]))`
beside `:host([placement="end"])` rather than as a value written here: a
default assigned to the property would reflect onto every host and put a

members.name: modal
members.description:
Whether the drawer blocks the page behind it.

Turning this off removes the focus trap and the scrim together, because
they are one decision: a panel that traps focus without covering the page
strands the reader, and one that covers without trapping lets them tab
behind the cover.

lost its focus trap because a consumer forgot a word would be worse than an
attribute on the host, and nothing selects on it: the scrim is rendered or
not, rather than shown or hidden by CSS.

members.description:
Whether this row holds the region's tab stop. Written by the stack.

A drill-down keeps one stop and moves within it on the arrows, so every

deeper or came back: the panel simply holds different words. Sliding in the
direction of travel says which happened, and it is most of the reason this is
a component rather than a menu with its trigger removed.

An animation rather than a transition, because there is nothing to transition
from: the page arriving was not in the DOM a frame ago. Under
`prefers-reduced-motion` it becomes the instant swap `Menu` does.

members.name: loading
members.description:

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText

members.name: emptyText

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus

The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: items
members.description: The rows on the page showing, which is what the keys move over.

members.name: placeTabStop
members.description:
Puts the region's one tab stop on the first row of the page showing.

Every row rendered at `-1`, so nothing in the region was tab-reachable and
the keyboard could not get in at all without a pointer first. One row holds
the stop and the arrows move within, which is the roving pattern the
toolbar uses and the one a `menu` wants.

Called after every update, because the set changes with the page: drilling
in replaces the rows outright, and the stop has to land on rows that are
actually showing.

members.name: enter
members.description: Shows a row's page, and puts focus on the first row of it.

members.name: back
members.description:
Returns one page, and reports whether there was one to return to.

Focus lands on the row that opened the page being left, which is why the
row is read before going back rather than after: a reader who drills in and
comes straight out should be on the row they pressed, not at the top of a
list they have already read.

members.name: mark
members.description: Walks the tree marking which rows are on the page showing.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.description:
The field is a box rather than a line, because nothing is typed into it: its
height is not a line of text, and what a reader aims at is the whole area. The
border is dashed for the same reason a drop target usually is, which is the
only affordance one has before anything is being dragged.

The native input is kept and laid over the field at zero opacity rather than
hidden, so a click anywhere on the box lands on the input itself and opens the
picker. Hiding it with `display: none` would take it out of the tab order and
out of the form, and a script clicking a hidden input is the same thing with
more moving parts.

The focus ring is drawn on the field, because the control it belongs to is
invisible.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: accept
members.description: Which files the picker offers, as a native `accept` list.

members.name: multiple
members.description: Whether more than one file can be chosen.

members.name: capture
members.description: Which camera or microphone a mobile picker should offer, if any.

members.name: triggerLabel
members.description: What the trigger reads, where nothing is slotted into it.

members.name: locale
members.description: Language tag the sizes are written in. Absent uses the runtime's own.

members.name: removeLabel
members.description: What the control removing one file is called, per file.

members.name: dropping
members.description:
Whether something is being dragged over the field.

State rather than a property: it is a fact about a gesture in progress and
nothing a consumer sets. It reaches the stylesheet as `data-dropping` on an
element in this shadow root, never on the host, which is markup a consumer
rendered.

members.name: files
members.description:
The files chosen, which is the element's own and never assigned.

Read from the input rather than mirrored into a field. The input is what
the picker filled and what a form submits, so a copy here could only ever
disagree with it.

members.name: control
members.description:
The input, or nothing where there is no tree to ask.

The guard is for the server, whose element shim carries attributes but not
traversal: `render` reads `files`, `files` reads this, and an unguarded
`querySelector` threw before a single character of markup came out. Nothing
is lost by answering `null` there, because a file only ever arrives through
a reader and a server has never met one.

members.name: clear
members.description:
Takes every file back out.

The one change a consumer can ask for. Setting a `FileList` is refused by
every browser for a reason worth keeping, but emptying one is not: nothing
about the page learns anything it did not already have.

members.name: removeAt
members.description:
Drops one file, by index.

`removeAt` rather than `remove`, which is `Element`'s own and takes no
arguments: shadowing it would break every caller who meant the node.

Through `DataTransfer`, which is the only way to build a `FileList`: the
type has no constructor and `input.files` takes nothing else. It is the same
mechanism a drop uses, so a file put in by dragging and one put in by the
picker come back out the same way.

members.name: announce
members.description: Says what is now chosen, by name, and puts it in the form.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Reports the files and the validity the host stands behind.

`FormData` rather than a string, because a file input submits the file
itself and several of them under one name. The anchor on `setValidity` is
the input, so the browser's own bubble points at something a reader can see
rather than at a host with no text in it.

members.name: handleDragOver
members.description:
Takes a drop, which a bare file input can only do on itself.

The input is invisible here, so the field is the target and the files are
put into the input afterwards: that keeps one source of truth, and it is
what makes a dropped file and a picked file indistinguishable to a form.

`preventDefault` on dragover as well as on drop, because without it the
browser navigates to the file and the page is gone.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts focus on the input, the way a label pointing at one would.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description: Empties it, which is what a form reset means for a file input.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

declarations.description:

`min` fills as many equal columns as fit above that width, which is a
responsive layout with no breakpoint to maintain. Setting `min` wins, because

members.name: columns
members.description: Fixed number of equal columns.

members.name: min
members.description:
Minimum column width, filling as many as fit.

Takes precedence over `columns`: a grid that both fixes a count and reflows
is two intentions in one element.

members.name: gap
members.description: Space between cells, named on the space scale.

members.name: align

members.name: applyTemplate
members.description:
Writes the track list into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, and the difference is
hydration. An inline style on the host is an attribute the element gives
itself once it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup does not have
it and hydration reports a mismatch it will not patch up. The shadow root
is not part of the tree React hydrates, so a rule written there is free.

The element is filled imperatively because Lit refuses expressions inside
`<style>`: it is an invalid binding location and throws while rendering
rather than at build time. Hence a static, empty element in the template
and its `textContent` set here.

It sets a custom property rather than the track list itself. A shadow
root's adopted stylesheets cascade *after* its own `<style>` elements, and
`static styles` is adopted, so a `grid-template-columns` here lost to the
one in the stylesheet and every `min` grid came out a single column. The
stylesheet only ever reads `--_grid-template`, so there is nothing to
lose against.

The consequence is that a server-rendered grid falls back to the
stylesheet's single column until it upgrades. That is why `columns` is also
expressed as plain CSS below: the fixed-count case, which can be enumerated,
needs no JavaScript at all, and only `min` depends on this.

`Card.Header` is part of a card, and an icon-only button is not part of a
button. It is a button with different content and a different shape, which
makes it its own component.

`ghost` is the resting state here rather than `outlined`, and is never

members.name: tone
members.description: What the button means, which decides its colour and nothing else.

members.name: shape
members.description:
The outline it is cut to, which is a third axis and not a fourth appearance.

`appearance` says how filled it is and `tone` says what it means; neither of
them says what shape it is, and folding a shape into either would put a
control's outline in the same word as its colour. A rounded square is the
resting one because that is what a control in a row of controls should be.

`circle` is the floating action button, and it is the reason this exists: a
round, raised, primary control holding the one action a screen is for. It is
a shape rather than a component, because a component would re-declare
`appearance`, `tone`, `label` and the size around a control that already has
them, and because the same shape is wanted by an avatar's overlay, a media
control and a map's own buttons. Where it sits is the page's business: see
`data-dock` in the base layer.

members.description:

Separate from `shape`, because they are separate facts: a docked control is
raised whatever its outline, and a circle inside a toolbar is not raised at
all. Shadow rather than a border, since what is under a floating control is
the page and a line drawn on the page is not the same as being above it.

The mapping differs by one, because this control rests as a ghost:
`tertiary` is the resting state here, and `danger` is a red mark on it
rather than a filled red square.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: isDisabled
members.description:
Whether the control is off, by its own attribute or by an ancestor.

What a component should bind to rather than `disabled`, which is only the
half of it the consumer wrote.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description: The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.
