Asks each child for its own focus target rather than matching tag names, so
a toolbar holds anything, including elements this package has never heard
of. Client only: there is no tree to walk on the server.

members.name: setTabStop
members.description:
Moves the single tab stop to one control.

Prefers the control's own `focusable` property to writing `tabindex` on it.
The attribute is a change to markup the consumer rendered, which a React
consumer's hydration reports and does not patch up; a control that offers
the property moves the stop inside its own shadow root instead.

`tabindex` stays as the fallback, because a toolbar has to hold controls
this package has never heard of.

members.name: claimTabStop
members.description:
Sets the first tab stop once every custom control has upgraded.

A custom element has no properties at all before it upgrades, so a pass
that ran first would find no `focusable`, take the `tabindex` fallback, and
write the very attribute this exists to avoid.

members.name: restoreTabStop
members.description:
Gives the tab stop back to a control that still exists.

`controls` excludes anything disabled or hidden, so disabling the control
holding the stop dropped it out of the list while every other control was
already at `-1`. The toolbar then had no tab stop at all and the keyboard
could not reach it again, from a change as ordinary as a Save button
disabling itself once the form is clean.

`foreign` stays false, the same as the first claim: a control this package
has never heard of that was never given `tabindex="-1"` is still in the
document's own tab order, so it is never the one that gets stranded.

members.description:

so a reflected default cannot appear on the host after hydration.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back controlled and stop responding. `data-open` carries the resolved
state for stylesheets, which is what it has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: openMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `open` by the time of the first update,
which is where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's
initial properties have all landed and nothing else has happened yet.

Decided once, because the alternative is deciding continuously, and that
was tried: taking any write as a claim of ownership meant an uncontrolled
element became controlled the moment a script assigned to it, or the
moment the component set its own state, and then stopped responding. Both
were real and neither is anything a consumer asked for. A mode is a
declaration, and a declaration is made once.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-open` or
`helix-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. In uncontrolled mode the
element then updates itself; in controlled mode it applies nothing and
waits for the consumer to pass a new `open`, which is what "controlled"
means.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: content
members.description:
The text shown in the bubble.

The common case, and the fallback for the `content` slot: slot something
there and it replaces this. Both cannot show at once, which is the point
of using fallback content rather than rendering whichever is present.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the element this describes, in this tooltip's own tree.

Set it and the tooltip stops wrapping: it renders no trigger, listens on
the element it names, and points its bubble there. Leave it unset and the
default slot is the trigger, which is the older form.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a tooltip inside another component's
shadow root names an element in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, which is
worth knowing before someone reads the DOM and thinks it did not take.
Measured against React 19.2.8: `for` exists on the prototype, so React sets
`element.for = 'save'` and writes nothing to the markup, where `content`
and `placement`, which are not properties on the class at that moment, come
through as attributes. Both paths reach the same place through Lit, so
nothing is broken by it; a `[for]` selector would find nothing, which is
why this does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: placement
members.description: Preferred side. It moves if that side does not fit.

members.name: offset
members.description:
Space between the trigger and the bubble, in pixels.

Eight, which used to be the size of the arrow the styled tier drew so the
point could reach the trigger while the bubble did not. **The arrow is
gone**, and the number stays: it is now simply the gap, and eight is what
reads as beside rather than attached at every placement. Nothing depends on
it any more, so a consumer changing it changes the gap and nothing else.

members.name: disabled
members.description: Whether the tooltip never shows.

members.name: delay
members.description:
How long the pointer must rest before the bubble appears, in milliseconds.

Without one, sweeping across a row of controls flashes a tooltip for each
of them, which is noise rather than help. Focus opens with no delay: a
keyboard reader arriving on a control has already committed to it.

members.name: delayOut
members.description: How long the bubble stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds.

members.name: holds
members.description:
What is currently keeping the bubble up.

The pointer and focus are two holders and they shared one timer with
nothing counting them, so whichever left last won: moving the pointer off a
control that still had keyboard focus scheduled a hide and took the bubble
away from under the reader. The same fault the toast timer had, and the
same answer.

members.name: trigger
members.description:
The element the bubble points at.

The trigger, not the host. The host is `display: contents` so it wraps
without adding a box, and an element that generates no box measures as
nothing at the document origin: the bubble was placed against the corner
of the viewport rather than against the button.

members.name: named
members.description:
The element `for` names, or null.

`getRootNode()` rather than `document`, which is what makes this work inside
another component: an id is unique to a tree, and a tooltip in a shadow root
names an element in that root. Client only, since the server has no tree to
search.

members.name: bubbleLayer
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, /* Annotated, because without it the array's element type is inferred from `this`, whose own type depends on this controller, and TypeScript stops at the cycle. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null)[] => [this, this.named], offset: () => this.offset, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="tooltip"]'), })

members.name: hasContent
members.description: Whether there is anything to show. Asked of the slot rather than of the property, because either can carry the content. `assignedNodes` without `flatten` answers what the consumer provided and not what the fallback would render, which is exactly the question: a bubble with only fallback and an empty property is empty. Text or an element, because neither alone is the test. An element on its own would count ` ` as something to say, and text on its own would count an icon as nothing, when an icon is the whole point of slotting rather than setting the property. Client only. The server has no assignment to inspect, and nothing calls this there: a tooltip opens in response to a pointer or to focus.

members.name: describedText
members.description:
The bubble's words as a plain string, for naming the host.

The property when it is set, otherwise whatever was slotted, flattened.
Rich content collapses to its text, which is the right answer for a
description: `Save ⌘ S` is what a reader needs, not the markup.

members.name: handleContentChange
members.description:
Re-links the description when what is in the bubble changes.

`updated` alone is not enough: content arriving from the light DOM changes
no property here, so nothing would schedule the update that re-reads it. A
consumer rendering the bubble's content after this upgrades, which is what
a framework does, would leave the trigger describing nothing.

members.name: show
members.description: Shows the bubble, unless there is nothing to show.

members.name: hide
members.description: Hides the bubble.

members.name: showLater
members.description: Shows after the pointer has rested for `delay`.

members.name: hideLater
members.description: Hides after `delayOut`, so crossing the gap to the bubble does not close it.

members.name: release
members.description: Hides only once nothing is holding the bubble up.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Escape closes the bubble from wherever the reader is.

On the document, not on the host, which is where it was: a tooltip opened
by hover has focus somewhere else entirely, so the press never reached this
element and Escape worked only for the one case that needed it least. That
is the case the pattern names, a reader escaping a tooltip obscuring what
is under it, and it was the case that did nothing.

Not stopped from propagating: a tooltip is not what the reader was trying
to escape if it sits inside something else that also closes.

members.name: bound
members.description:
What the pointer and focus listeners are currently on.

Held, rather than recomputed at removal time, because what `for` names can
change: unbinding from wherever the element is *now* leaves a live listener
on wherever it was, and a tooltip that opens from a control it no longer
describes is worse than one that does not open at all.

members.name: bind
members.description:
Puts the listeners on whatever the trigger is.

The host when it wraps, since the trigger is inside it and both `focusin`
and `focusout` bubble. The named element when `for` is set, because then the
host wraps nothing and `pointerenter` does not bubble at all.

Client only, and after the first render: `for` names an element that may not
have upgraded, or existed, when this one connected.

members.name: audited
members.description: Said once per element, however many times it opens.

members.name: auditDescription
members.description:
Checks that the trigger actually points back, and says so once if not.

`for` is only half a link: this element finds the trigger, and the trigger
has to name this element for a screen reader to read the two together. That
second half is the consumer's line to write, deliberately, because writing
it from here means `setAttribute` on markup they server-rendered. So it is
theirs to forget, and a silent accessibility gap is the worst kind: the
tooltip looks completely correct.

On first open rather than on connect, because a framework may render the
attribute after this element upgrades, and because a tooltip that never
opens has described nothing eitherway.

Either attribute counts. WebAwesome uses `aria-labelledby` over
`aria-describedby` on purpose, their reasoning being that some screen
readers want the description on the focusable element itself while a label
reads on first focus regardless, and that is a live enough question that
this should not be the thing to settle it.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: value
members.description: Identifies the item to the consumer, carried in `helix-select`.

members.name: href
members.description:
Where this node goes, which makes its row a real link.

Unset by default, and unreflected: a tree of choosable nodes is not a tree
of links, and an empty `href` written onto every row would be a link to the
current page on every item a consumer never asked to be one.

members.name: target
members.description: Where the link opens, for the rare row that leaves the site.

members.name: rel
members.description:
What the link declares about where it goes.

Set by the consumer rather than derived from `target`: `noreferrer` is a
decision about their own analytics and a component should not make it for
them. `noopener` is not needed as a default either, since every browser
this library supports implies it for `target="_blank"` already.

members.name: selected
members.description:
Whether this item is the current one.

Not reflected, for the reason `level` below gives in full: the tree assigns
this after it upgrades, so the attribute would be a change to markup the
consumer rendered and hydration would report it. It reflected, one line
from the paragraph saying why it must not.

The stylesheet reads it from the row inside this shadow root, which is the
answer `level` gives one paragraph down: the indent it drives is written
onto the row rather than onto the host, because the row is not part of the
tree React hydrates. Mirroring to `data-selected` on the host instead was
the same fault with a different name, and React said so.

members.name: level
members.description:
Depth from the root, set by the tree so indentation needs no CSS nesting.

Not reflected. The tree assigns this after it upgrades, so an attribute
here would be a change to markup the consumer rendered and hydration would
report it. The indent it drives is written onto the row instead, inside the
shadow root, which is not part of the tree React hydrates.

members.name: focusable
members.description: Whether this item holds the tree's single tab stop.

members.name: branch
members.description: Whether anything is slotted into `children`. Read after first render.

members.name: isBranch
members.description: Whether this node has children.

members.name: focusItem
members.description:
Moves focus to this node.

Which element that is moves with `href`: the thing carrying `treeitem` is
the thing the tree's roving tab stop lives on, and with a link that is the
row rather than the wrapper around it.

members.name: select
members.description: Selects this node and announces it.

members.name: activate
members.description:
Chooses this node the way a reader does, from a press or from Enter.

Selecting and following are two things and this is where they meet, so the
pointer and the keyboard take one path to the same end. The tree calls this
rather than `select` for the keyboard, which is what fixes Enter: a nav
tree whose rows are links could be walked with the arrows and not entered,
because choosing announced a value and nothing listened for it.

members.name: follow
members.description:
Follows a link slotted into the name, if there is one.

A row is wider than the words in it: the indent, the padding, and with the
chevron at the far end most of the row's width are all outside the anchor,
so a reader who pressed the row anywhere but on the text got nothing. The
words are the consumer's own content and this does not rewrite them, so
what it does instead is press the link they put there.

The consumer's anchor rather than an `href` of this element's own,
deliberately: a framework's link component is what carries prefetching and
client-side routing, and a plain `<a href>` rendered in here would be a
full page load on a site that had neither. A synthetic click is what those
components listen for, so both keep working.

`querySelector` on the light DOM, not the render root: the link is the
consumer's, and it is scoped to this item's own name rather than to the
whole subtree, or a branch would follow the first link belonging to one of
its children.

members.name: renderRow
members.description: Everything inside the row, which is the same whichever element it is.

members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:
Which end of the row the branch chevron sits at.

Styled tier, because it is presentation and nothing else: it moves paint
and leaves the markup, the ARIA and the reading order exactly as they were.
It was written on the base class first, which the tier rule forbids for
precisely this kind of property.

On the tree rather than on the item, because it is a fact about the list. A
navigation puts every chevron on the same side, and a per-item version
would make a ragged tree writable and would have to be repeated on every
row to say one thing.

**Optional, with no default.** A reflected property that defaults to a
value writes that value onto every host: `chevron-placement="start"`
appeared in the server's markup for every tree anybody rendered, which is
the same fault `href` and `target` had on `Button`. The resting arrangement
is the absence of the attribute, and the stylesheet only asks about `end`.

It is worth owning rather than leaving to `::part(toggle)`, which a
consumer could reach for: the naive version is `order` plus an auto margin,
and the row's `end` slot already carries an auto margin of its own, so the
two split the free space and the chevron lands halfway along. Measured at
70px short. That is the kind of thing a component should absorb once.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: rows

members.name: countRows
members.description:

count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.description:

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description: Initial item for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: activeMode
members.description:
Whether the consumer owns the state, decided once and then fixed.

Read off whether anything had set `active` by the first update, which is
where markup, a hydrating server's attributes and a framework's initial
properties have all landed. See `MixinControllerOpen` for why this is
decided once rather than continuously.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the tree.

members.name: items
members.description:
Every item, in the order a reader moving down would meet them.

Selected by tag rather than by walking everything and filtering. `'*'` built
an array of every descendant element in the tree, labels and icons and
whatever a consumer slotted into a row included, and threw most of it away;
on a tree of any size that is the array a single arrow press rebuilds.

The two tag names rather than `instanceof` on everything: a styled
`helix-tree-item` extends the base, so both names are needed, and the
`instanceof` stays as the type guard because a consumer can write either

members.name: visibleItems
members.description: Items a reader can actually reach: not inside a collapsed branch.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.

members.name: handleBranch
members.description:
A branch opened or closed, whoever did it.

The keyboard paths called `syncItems` by hand and the pointer path did not,
so collapsing a branch by clicking its chevron left the tab stop on a row
inside the subtree that had just been hidden: the tree kept its one stop
and the stop was on something nobody could see or reach. Listening for the
item's own open events covers every way a branch can move, including a
consumer setting `open` directly.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

declarations.description:
The player is the base tier's. What this adds is the bar: where it sits, when
it is there, and what the two ranges look like, which is the whole reason to
replace a control set that cannot be styled.

**The bar is over the picture, not under it.** A bar in the layout would move
everything below the video by its own height and would leave a strip of page
colour under a picture that is meant to be the whole of it. Over it, the
video is the component's size and the controls belong to it.

**It goes when nobody is using it, and comes back for the keyboard.** Hidden
once a playing video has gone `idle-delay` without being touched, shown again
the moment the pointer moves, and shown whenever anything inside it has
focus, which is what keeps it reachable without a pointer. A paused video
keeps its bar, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.

Whether the browser draws the controls instead of this element.

A fallback rather than a default. Two bars over one video is worse than
either alone, so this one is not drawn at all when it is set.

members.name: preload
members.description: How much to fetch before anything is asked for.

members.name: extraControls
members.description:
Controls beyond the ones every player has, named in the order they appear.

A list rather than a property apiece. A bar is a row with a budget, and a
boolean per feature invites a consumer to switch all of them on: naming
them makes the row a decision, and makes the order theirs. Anything
unrecognised is skipped rather than throwing, since the list is markup and
a typo should cost a control, not a page.

`pip` is offered only where the platform has it, checked rather than
assumed: it is absent on iPhone and behind a flag in Firefox, and a button
that cannot work is worse than one that is not there.

The names are `speed`, `pip`, `remote` and `download`.

**`download` is named and never assumed.** Offering the file is a decision
about the content rather than about the player, and plenty of consumers
decline it deliberately. It is also the one control whose success is not
ours to promise: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, so a file served
from somewhere else opens rather than saves, which is the browser's rule
and not something a player can work around.

members.name: overflowControls
members.description:
Controls that go behind one button instead of onto the bar, named the same
way.

**Named rather than measured, and the reason is that a width cannot answer
this.** A media query asks about the window, and the bar's problem is its
own width: a video in a 320px sidebar on a desktop is cramped and a
full-bleed hero on a phone is not. A container query asks the right
question and still cannot answer it, because how many controls there are is
the consumer's, so the threshold is not a width but a width per control,
which is a guess. And a control that moves between the bar and a hidden
menu as the layout shifts is a control the reader has to find twice.

So the consumer says where the fold is, which they can, having already
named the controls in order. A name in both lists is drawn once, on the
bar: two of the same control is worse than either placement.

members.name: startControl
members.description:
The big mark over the picture before anything has played, or `none`.

**On unless it is turned off, because a stopped video has nothing else.**
Measured on the bar as it was: the play glyph is 16 by 16 in a 24 by 24
target, which is 0.12% of a 528 by 396 picture and 0.33% at 320. What a
reader meets first is a still frame with some chrome along the bottom, and
nothing in it says "press to watch".

`none` is for the cases where that is wrong rather than right: a muted loop
behind a hero, a grid of eight thumbnails, anything where the video is
decoration rather than something to start.

**Only before the first play.** A video paused halfway already has its bar
up, because a paused video never idles, so the small control is visible and
the reader has just used it. Covering the picture they stopped to look at
would be the opposite of helpful.

A value rather than a boolean, so the resting state is the attribute's
absence: a boolean defaulting to on would have to be spelled as its own
negation.

members.name: localFile
members.description:
Whether the file this points at is ours to hand over.

`blob:` and `data:` named rather than compared, because the rule `download`
actually follows is same-origin *or one of those two*: a clip a consumer
generated in the page has no origin to match and is theirs to save by
definition. Comparing origins alone called both foreign, so the one case
where a download certainly works was the one case it was not offered.

members.name: speeds
members.description: The speeds offered, slowest first, as multipliers of normal.

members.name: idleDelay
members.description:
How long the bar waits after the pointer stops before it goes, in ms.

It used to leave the moment the pointer did, which is not how a player
behaves: a reader moving across the picture to reach a control watched it
vanish under them. Zero turns the wait off and the bar goes immediately;
a large number keeps it up for as long as anyone is likely to look.

The wait is only ever about *idling*. A video that is paused keeps its bar
regardless, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.

members.name: playLabel
members.description: What the play control is called while it would start the video.

members.name: pauseLabel
members.description: And while it would stop it.

members.name: loadingLabel
members.description: What a reader is told while the picture is waiting for more of itself.

members.name: errorLabel
members.description: And what they are told when it will not play at all.

members.name: buffering
members.description:
Whether playback has stopped to wait for data.

**Only ever after somebody asked for playback**, which is what `waiting`
means: the element wanted the next frame and did not have it. Before that,
a video that has loaded nothing is a poster with a play control over it,
which looks deliberate and is. A spinner there would say something is
happening when nothing is, on every video on the page.

The case this covers is the one that looks like a bug: a picture frozen
mid-play, the scrubber stopped, and nothing on screen saying why.

members.name: failed
members.description: Whether the source failed, which is the other thing a frozen frame can mean.

members.name: cue
members.description:
The cue on screen now, as nodes, or nothing between cues.

Nodes rather than a string, because `VTTCue.text` is the cue's *source*:
WebVTT carries markup, and a caption file in the wild is full of it. `<v
Hildy>` names who is speaking, `<b>` and `<i>` and `<u>` mark emphasis, and
`<c.loud>` classes a line. Rendered as text every one of those arrives on
screen as visible angle brackets.

`getCueAsHTML` is the platform parsing its own format, so nothing here has
to know the grammar and no cue text is ever treated as HTML: what comes
back is a fragment the browser built, not a string anybody interpolated.

members.name: idle
members.description: Whether the reader has been still long enough for the bar to go.

members.name: remoteConnected
members.description: Whether it is playing somewhere else right now.

members.name: remoteWatch
members.description: Cancels the availability watch, since it outlives a single render.

members.name: offers
members.description: Whether this platform can do a named control at all.

members.name: extras
members.description: The extras asked for, in order, and only the ones this platform can do.

members.name: overflow
members.description:
The controls asked for behind the overflow button, in order.

A name in both lists is on the bar and not here. Drawing it twice is worse
than either placement, and the bar is the one a reader can see.

members.name: media
members.description: The sources and caption tracks to copy into the video, as the consumer wrote them.

members.name: play
members.description:
Starts playing, where the platform allows it.

The rejection is swallowed on purpose: a browser refuses `play()` when
nothing the reader did asked for it, and that is a policy answer rather than
a fault. What follows a refused play is a paused player showing its start
control, which is the correct thing to be looking at.

members.name: pause
members.description: Stops, leaving the frame up.

members.name: toggle
members.description: Toggles playback, which is what every key and the button both come to.

members.name: seek
members.description: Moves to a point in seconds, clamped to what exists.

members.name: handleMedia
members.description:
Rebuilds the copies from whatever the consumer has slotted.

The attribute list is explicit rather than a blind copy of every attribute:
these are two elements with a known and small surface, and copying anything
a consumer happened to put on one would carry their framework's own markers
into a shadow root that has no use for them.

members.name: handleWaiting
members.description:
Relayed, because none of these cross a shadow boundary on their own.

The video is inside this element's shadow root, so a consumer listening on
the element they wrote hears nothing at all without this. Input relays
`change` for the same reason.

members.name: claimSession
members.description:
Takes the page's media session, and tells the platform what is playing.

On play rather than on render, which is the ownership rule: a page with two
players gives the session to whichever one the reader started, so a
headset's buttons land on what they are listening to rather than on
whichever came first in the markup.

The handlers are what make a headset's play, pause and skip work at all.
Without them a platform falls back to guessing which element was meant,
which is right often enough to hide the fault and wrong exactly when there
are two.

members.name: handleCue
members.description:
Draws the active cue ourselves, so it can be put where we want it.

The browser renders cues inside the video's own box and there is no
standard way to inset that box: a caption lands under the control bar and
stays there. `::cue` styles the text and not the region, and the property
that moves the region is a `-webkit-` internal that two of the three
engines do not have.

So the track is set to `hidden` rather than `showing`, which is the mode
that keeps the cues coming without drawing them, and what it reports is
rendered into a part of our own. That also makes captions styleable, which
`::cue` only half allows.

members.name: toggleCaptions
members.description: Turns the first caption track on or off, which is what the button means.

members.name: skip
members.description:
Says the reader asked for another item, and does nothing else.

There is nothing else it could do. A `<video>` plays one resource, so what
comes before or after it is a fact this element does not hold: a playlist
has it, or the consumer does. Announcing is the whole of the contribution,
and the event bubbles so a wrapper hears it.

The same call answers the button, the row in the overflow menu, and the
skip keys on a headset, which is why the media session's handlers point
here rather than at anything of their own.

members.name: cycleSpeed
members.description: Steps through the speeds offered, which is what one button can do.

members.name: watchRemote
members.description:
Starts watching for something to play this on, and stops on the way out.

The Remote Playback API is the standard one, and it is what Safari
implements for AirPlay and Chrome for Cast: one call covers both, where the
older `webkitShowPlaybackTargetPicker` covers only the first. Firefox has
neither, and `remote` simply being absent is what turns the control off
there.

`watchAvailability` returns an id that has to be cancelled, or the callback
outlives the element that owns it.

members.name: promptRemote
members.description: Opens the platform's own device picker. It has no list of its own.

members.name: toggleFullscreen
members.description:
Into fullscreen and back, and quiet about being refused.

`requestFullscreen` rejects rather than returning false, and the two
refusals a consumer will actually meet are a Permissions Policy that does
not grant `fullscreen` to the frame the player is in, and a call without
user activation. Both are `TypeError: Permissions check failed`, which is
the same message for two different causes.

It was `void`ed, so a refusal became an unhandled rejection: the button did
nothing and said nothing, and the console entry it left named neither the
element nor the reason. Caught here, the state stays honest because
`aria-pressed` follows `fullscreenchange` rather than this call, so a
refused request leaves a button that correctly reports "not fullscreen".

members.name: stir
members.description:
Restarts the wait, on anything that counts as the reader being here.

Pointer movement and focus both count, and both have to: a reader using the
keyboard never moves a pointer, and a bar that only answered the mouse
would leave them nothing to look at.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys every player uses, bound to this element rather than the document.

A video is not a command palette: its keys belong to it while a reader is
on it, and a page with two videos on it would otherwise have both answering
the same press.

Nothing is taken while focus is in a range. The scrubber and the volume are
real inputs and the arrows are already theirs, so intercepting would mean
seeking twice for one press.

members.name: renderExtra
members.description:
One named control, as a button on the bar.

A method rather than four branches inlined, because the same four names are
asked for twice now, once for the bar and once for the menu behind it, and
two lists that have to stay in step is how a control ends up offered in one
place and not the other.

members.name: renderOverflowItem
members.description:
The same control as a row in the overflow menu.

The label is words rather than a mark, which is the difference between a
bar and a menu: a row has the width for a name and a reader scanning one is
reading rather than recognising. `download` is a linked row, which is what
`Menu.Item`'s `href` is for.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: appearance
attributes.description: Whether the bar floats on the picture or sits on its own ground.

attributes.name: src
attributes.description: Where the video is, for the common case of one file.

attributes.name: poster
attributes.description: A still shown before it plays, which the platform draws itself.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name, since a video is not described by its filename.

attributes.name: loop
attributes.description: Whether it starts again at the end.

attributes.name: muted
attributes.description: Whether it starts silent, which is what an autoplaying video must do.

attributes.name: plays-inline
attributes.description: Whether it plays where it sits rather than taking over the screen.

attributes.name: controls
attributes.description:
Whether the browser draws the controls instead of this element.

A fallback rather than a default. Two bars over one video is worse than
either alone, so this one is not drawn at all when it is set.

attributes.name: preload
attributes.description: How much to fetch before anything is asked for.

attributes.name: extra-controls
attributes.description:
Controls beyond the ones every player has, named in the order they appear.

A list rather than a property apiece. A bar is a row with a budget, and a
boolean per feature invites a consumer to switch all of them on: naming
them makes the row a decision, and makes the order theirs. Anything
unrecognised is skipped rather than throwing, since the list is markup and
a typo should cost a control, not a page.

`pip` is offered only where the platform has it, checked rather than
assumed: it is absent on iPhone and behind a flag in Firefox, and a button
that cannot work is worse than one that is not there.

The names are `speed`, `pip`, `remote` and `download`.

**`download` is named and never assumed.** Offering the file is a decision
about the content rather than about the player, and plenty of consumers
decline it deliberately. It is also the one control whose success is not
ours to promise: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, so a file served
from somewhere else opens rather than saves, which is the browser's rule
and not something a player can work around.

attributes.name: overflow-controls
attributes.description:
Controls that go behind one button instead of onto the bar, named the same
way.

**Named rather than measured, and the reason is that a width cannot answer
this.** A media query asks about the window, and the bar's problem is its
own width: a video in a 320px sidebar on a desktop is cramped and a
full-bleed hero on a phone is not. A container query asks the right
question and still cannot answer it, because how many controls there are is
the consumer's, so the threshold is not a width but a width per control,
which is a guess. And a control that moves between the bar and a hidden
menu as the layout shifts is a control the reader has to find twice.

So the consumer says where the fold is, which they can, having already
named the controls in order. A name in both lists is drawn once, on the
bar: two of the same control is worse than either placement.

attributes.name: start-control
attributes.description:
The big mark over the picture before anything has played, or `none`.

**On unless it is turned off, because a stopped video has nothing else.**
Measured on the bar as it was: the play glyph is 16 by 16 in a 24 by 24
target, which is 0.12% of a 528 by 396 picture and 0.33% at 320. What a
reader meets first is a still frame with some chrome along the bottom, and
nothing in it says "press to watch".

`none` is for the cases where that is wrong rather than right: a muted loop
behind a hero, a grid of eight thumbnails, anything where the video is
decoration rather than something to start.

**Only before the first play.** A video paused halfway already has its bar
up, because a paused video never idles, so the small control is visible and
the reader has just used it. Covering the picture they stopped to look at
would be the opposite of helpful.

A value rather than a boolean, so the resting state is the attribute's
absence: a boolean defaulting to on would have to be spelled as its own
negation.

attributes.name: speeds
attributes.description: The speeds offered, slowest first, as multipliers of normal.

attributes.name: idle-delay
attributes.description:
How long the bar waits after the pointer stops before it goes, in ms.

It used to leave the moment the pointer did, which is not how a player
behaves: a reader moving across the picture to reach a control watched it
vanish under them. Zero turns the wait off and the bar goes immediately;
a large number keeps it up for as long as anyone is likely to look.

The wait is only ever about *idling*. A video that is paused keeps its bar
regardless, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.
